ff.title: Frankfurt's theory
ff.lead: The American philosopher Harry G. Frankfurt wrote an essay in 1986 (published as a book in 2005) that made the topic a subject of serious analysis.
ff.core.p: A liar <mark>knows the truth</mark> and deliberately departs from it. A bullshitter, in contrast, <mark>does not care whether it is true</mark>: what matters is the impression of being convincing, well informed or likable.
ff.r3.liar: Can be exposed once the truth comes out
ff.r3.bs: Works even when what is said happens to be true
ff.r4.liar: The credibility of one specific claim
ff.lab.p: Set how much the speaker cares about the truth, and whether they say what they believe is true.
ff.truthful: Says what they believe is true
ff.role.honest.d: Cares about the truth and says what they believe is true.
ff.role.liar.d: Cares about the truth but deliberately says something else. This is still a game played by the rules of truth: the liar lies because it matters what is true.
ff.role.bs.d: Hardly cares whether what they say is true. Whether it turns out true by accident is beside the point; the impression is what counts. That is why the other switch no longer matters.
ff.why.p: A liar still plays by the rules of truth. A bullshitter walks out of the game, so when it spreads, the yardstick for measuring statements disappears. Frankfurt argues that bullshit is a greater enemy of the truth than lies are.
ty.title: Types of bullshit
ty.lead: Empty talk comes in many forms. The scale shows how hard each one is to recognize.
ty.pseudo.d: Sentences that sound deep but mean nothing. In a 2015 study by Pennycook and colleagues, many people rated randomly assembled sentences of this kind as profound.
ty.pseudo.ex: Consciousness is the motionless unfolding of possibility.
ty.corp.d: A pile-up of fashionable terms: synergy, scalability, paradigm shift. It conveys no information but signals expertise.
ty.corp.ex: We proactively align stakeholder expectations with strategic direction.
ty.pol.d: Statements that dodge the question and retreat into generalities. The goal is the impression, not a precise answer.
ty.pol.ex: “Will taxes go up?” “What matters is that we put families first.”
ty.day.d: When someone offers an opinion on a subject they know little about because they feel they have to say something. Frankfurt argues that one main source of bullshit is the feeling that one is obliged to speak.
ty.day.ex: Everybody knows that studies are wrong anyway.
det.title: Bullshit detector
det.lead: Paste a text. The detector measures the share of fashionable jargon and also takes concrete numbers into account. It is a game, not a real analysis.
det.ph: E.g. We holistically scale the synergistic value chain…
det.hint: Concrete numbers and dates lower the score because they make a statement checkable.

quiz.title: Quiz: empty or meaningful?
quiz.lead: Eight sentences are coming. Decide whether each one is bullshit or carries real information.
quiz.r.low: Keep practicing: have a look at the Types and Defense pages.
quiz.r.mid: You have a good eye, but the trickier ones still fool you.
quiz.q1.t: We proactively leverage cross-functional synergies to unlock stakeholder value.
quiz.q1.w: Plenty of fashionable words but no concrete claim: who does what, by when?
quiz.q2.t: The meeting moved to Thursday at 10 because the room was double-booked.
quiz.q2.w: Concrete, checkable information: when and why it changed.
quiz.q3.t: Awareness is the unfolding of silent potential.
quiz.q3.w: It sounds deep, but it asserts nothing you could check (pseudo-profound bullshit).
quiz.q4.t: At higher altitude air pressure is lower, so water boils at a lower temperature.
quiz.q4.w: A real explanation that is testable and true.
quiz.q5.t: Our paradigm shift strengthens a holistic ecosystem of scalable innovation.
quiz.q5.w: A heap of jargon: it fits almost anything, so it says nothing.
quiz.q6.t: I don't know the answer right now, but I'll look into it and get back to you tomorrow.
quiz.q6.w: Honest and concrete: it admits a gap in knowledge and commits to a step. That is the opposite of bullshit.
quiz.q7.t: Every challenge is an opportunity wrapped in the energy of change.
quiz.q7.w: A motivational platitude: pleasant to hear, but it claims nothing.
quiz.q8.t: The bridge has been closed since Monday, so take the northern road.
quiz.q8.w: Simple, concrete guidance. It can be checked and tells you what to do.
work.title: Corporate bullshit
work.lead: Organizations are a particularly comfortable home for empty talk, because appearances often count for more than substance.
work.bingo.p: Tap the words as you hear them in your next meeting. Four in a row, column or diagonal is a bingo.
work.bingo.words: synergy,paradigm shift,scalable,proactive,holistic,agile,stakeholders,added value,going forward,circle back,ecosystem,at the end of the day,low-hanging fruit,deep dive,touchpoint,win-win,alignment,end-to-end solution,take it offline,optimization,digital transformation,mission-critical,strategic,best practice
work.why.1: Speaking up is expected, even when someone has nothing to say.
work.why.2: A vague sentence is hard to hold anyone to, which makes it convenient.
work.why.3: Jargon signals belonging to the group.
work.why.4: Executive summaries and slide decks reward impression over substance.
work.graeber: David Graeber's 2018 book Bullshit Jobs argues that some paid jobs exist that even the people holding them cannot justify. Where there is no real task, a lot of words are needed to keep up appearances.
work.fix.p: Ask for specifics. If the answer stays general, that is the problem itself. The key question:
def.title: Defending against bullshit
def.lead: Counter-arguing is costly, so it pays to choose carefully when to step in.
def.list.p: Tick what you already do. Your progress is saved to your account.
def.s1: Ask for the point: “What exactly does that mean, with an example?”
def.s2: Ask for a source, out of curiosity rather than as an attack.
def.s3: Summarize it in your own words. If the speaker cannot confirm it, there was no content.
def.s4: Don't bullshit yourself. If you don't know, say: “I don't know.”
def.s5: Pick your battles: not every empty sentence deserves a debate.
def.s6: Ask for specifics: who, what, by when?
def.bl.p: The bullshit asymmetry principle says refuting nonsense takes an order of magnitude more energy than producing it. The slider illustrates this (an estimate, not a measurement).
def.bl.out: A {n}-word claim would need roughly {m} words to refute.
def.sum.p: Empty talk cannot be handled with the tools used against lies, because its problem is not that it is false but that it <mark>does not care about the truth</mark>. The antidote is patient, concrete questioning and keeping our own statements precise.
acc.title: Account and security
acc.lead: Manage your sign-in, two-step verification and active sessions here.
acc.2fa.p: Use an authenticator app (for example Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator or Aegis). When you sign in you will enter a 6-digit code in addition to your password.
acc.2fa.secret: Can't scan it? Enter this secret key in the app manually
acc.pw.done: Password changed. You were signed out on all other devices.
acc.out.p: If you are not sure you are signed out elsewhere, sign out everywhere.
acc.del.p: Your account and saved progress will be deleted permanently. Enter your password to confirm.
acc.del.confirm: Delete your account for good? This cannot be undone.
acc.prot.1: In transit: HTTPS (TLS 1.2 or newer) when a certificate is configured.
acc.prot.2: Password: scrypt hash with a unique salt; the password itself is never stored.
acc.prot.3: At rest: the whole data file is encrypted with AES-256-GCM.
acc.prot.4: Session: random ID in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie, expires after 30 minutes of inactivity.
acc.prot.5: Against attacks: CSRF tokens, a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) and attempt limiting.
